item.text: {"question_id":"8B.6","answer":"During the 2023 period, Sisi’s government converted some directives and programs into observable institutional practice, but implementation was uneven and evidence of quality, equity, and independent results is limited. Directly dated examples include the reported relocation of more than 100 government agencies, including 30 ministries and about 40,000 employees, to the New Administrative Capital, and presidential direction concerning court digitization and case processing; these figures come from official accounts and do not independently establish service quality, fairness, or budget performance (BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0018-E012). Anti-trafficking directives also produced specialized prosecution offices, judicial circuits, and training for more than 2,100 officials, but procedures were inconsistently used and victim services remained inadequate; the underlying prosecution figures primarily concern 2022 and the reporting period ending March 2023 (BATCH-0008-E005; BATCH-0008-E007). Government programs likewise had tangible reach: World Bank-supported measures helped maintain bread subsidies during December 2022–February 2023, and Universal Health Insurance had been rolled out in six governorates with more than 5 million reported enrollees and over 322 accredited providers, although implementation was shared with external partners and the figures are cumulative rather than 2023-only (BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0023-E003). Humanitarian arrangements at Rafah and Al-Arish in October–November 2023 also became operational, with food convoys and medical triage, evacuation, ambulances, and referral facilities, but the sources do not establish Sisi’s personal direction, sustained access, or patient outcomes (BATCH-0019-E008; BATCH-0018-E004). Conversely, major parts of the portfolio remained prospective or weakly implemented: the 2023 national dialogue produced no significant legal or political reforms; the government failed to open military companies to private investors and continued allocating land to the army; and the megaproject and housing agenda lacked necessary environmental studies, had poor occupancy and access evidence, and delivered only 215,000 of a planned one million affordable housing units in the earlier 2011–2016 project period (BATCH-0002-E003; BATCH-0009-R11-E010; BATCH-0009-R10-E009; BATCH-0009-R10-E010). Thus, plans clearly became practice in selected administrative, security, social-protection, health, judicial, and humanitarian domains, but substantial gaps, shared attribution, cumulative measures, and unverified official claims prevent treating implementation as consistently effective across the full
